knowledge_point.title: Rewriting a Double Integral Over a Circle or Part-Circle Not Centered at the Origin

question.:question/problem:
If $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,x^{2}+(y+1)^{2}\le 1\},$ then $\iint_D 1\,\mathrm{d}A=$

Choose the polar setup whose bounds describe $D$ with $r\ge 0$ and whose integrand is the given Cartesian integrand multiplied by the Jacobian $r.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint_D f(x,y)\,dA=\iint_\Delta f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta.
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186129275/plots/d825f39339e802647cd0-region.png)

Notice that the region $D$ represents the disk of radius $1$ centered at $(0,-1).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=r\cos\theta \\ y=r\sin\theta\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $x^{2}+(y+1)^{2}=1$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}x^{2}+(y+1)^{2}&=1\\(r\cos\theta)^2+(r\sin\theta+1)^2&=1\\r^2\cos^2\theta+r^2\sin^2\theta+2r\sin\theta+1&=1\\r^2(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)+2r\sin\theta&=0\\r^2+2r\sin\theta&=0\\r(r+2\sin\theta)&=0\end{aligned}
$$

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire circle, we must have $r=- 2 \sin{\left(\theta \right)}.$

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta.$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r=- 2 \sin{\left(\theta \right)}$ (at the boundary of the region):

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186129275/plots/d825f39339e802647cd0-radius.png)

Secondly, $\theta$ can vary between $\theta=\pi$ and $\theta=2 \pi.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186129275/plots/d825f39339e802647cd0-angle.png)

So, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta),$ the region can be expressed as

$$
\Delta=\{(r,\theta)\,:\,0\le r\le - 2 \sin{\left(\theta \right)},\,\pi\le\theta\le 2 \pi\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D 1\,dA&=\iint_\Delta (1)\,r\,dr\,d\theta\\&=\int_{\pi}^{2 \pi}\int_{0}^{- 2 \sin{\left(\theta \right)}}r\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: r ≥ 0; disk tangent to origin; radius integer/half ≤5

question.:question/problem:
If $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+(y-\frac{7}{2})^{2}\le \frac{49}{4}\},$ then ${∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A=$

Choose the polar setup whose bounds describe $D$ with $r\ge 0$ and whose integrand is the given Cartesian integrand multiplied by the Jacobian $r.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA={∬}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186129275/plots/e26b9bf6b6adb94cc508-region.png)

Notice that the region $D$ represents the disk of radius $\frac{7}{2\}$ centered at $(0,\frac{7}{2}).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+(y-\frac{7}{2})^{2}=\frac{49}{4\}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y-\frac{7}{2})^{2} & =\frac{49}{4} \\ {(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\frac{7}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{49}{4} \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -7r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{7}{2} & =\frac{49}{4} \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-7r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-7r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire circle, we must have $r=7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta .$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r=7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ (at the boundary of the region): 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186129275/plots/e26b9bf6b6adb94cc508-radius.png)

Secondly, $\theta $ can vary between $\theta =0$ (the positive $x$-axis) and $\theta =\pi $ (the negative $x$-axis):

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186129275/plots/e26b9bf6b6adb94cc508-angle.png)

So, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta \le \pi \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: r ≥ 0; disk tangent to origin; radius integer/half ≤5

question.:question/problem:
If $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,(x+\frac{7}{2})^{2}+{y}^{2}\le \frac{49}{4},\,y\le 0\},$ then ${∬}_{D}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A=$

Choose the polar setup whose bounds describe $D$ with $r\ge 0$ and whose integrand is the given Cartesian integrand multiplied by the Jacobian $r.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186129275/plots/28074b2e309a10137577-region.png)

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $\frac{7}{2\}$ centered at $(-\frac{7}{2},0).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${(x+\frac{7}{2})}^{2}+{y}^{2}=\frac{49}{4\}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x+\frac{7}{2})}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =\frac{49}{4} \\ {(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{7}{2})}^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =\frac{49}{4} \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +7r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{49}{4}+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =\frac{49}{4} \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+7r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}+7r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=-7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$ 

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta .$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r=-7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ (at the boundary of the region): 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186129275/plots/28074b2e309a10137577-radius.png)

Secondly, $\theta $ can vary between $\theta =\pi $ (the negative $x$-axis) and $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{2\}$ (the negative $y$-axis):

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186129275/plots/28074b2e309a10137577-angle.png)

So, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le -7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\pi \le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{-7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: r ≥ 0; disk tangent to origin; radius integer/half ≤5
